title: The definite article ال
summary: Arabic makes a noun definite by adding ال (al-) to the front, like "the" in English.
points: كِتَٰب means "a book"; ٱلْكِتَٰب means "the book".
In the Quran the alif of ال is often written ٱ (alif waṣla) because it is not pronounced when joined to the previous word.
Before "sun letters" such as ر, س, ن the ل is not pronounced: ٱلرَّحْمَٰن is read ar-raḥmān.

title: و — "and"
summary: The letter وَ (wa) means "and". It is attached directly to the front of the next word.
points: وَ is never written on its own; it joins the word after it.
It is the most frequent word in the Quran.
Spot it by looking for a word that starts with وَ and whose meaning starts with "and".

title: Small prepositions
summary: Short words like مِن (from), فِى (in), عَلَىٰ (on), إِلَىٰ (to) and عَن (about) link ideas together.
points: These words are extremely common — learning them unlocks a large share of every page.
Their exact English depends on context, so the same word may be translated slightly differently.
The noun after a preposition takes the genitive case, usually ending in -i.

title: Attached pronoun ـهُ (him / his / it)
summary: Arabic attaches pronouns to the end of words. ـهُ (-hu) means "him", "his" or "it".
points: رَبُّهُۥ = "his Lord" — the pronoun is joined to the noun.
After an i-sound it becomes ـهِ (-hi), as in بِهِۦ "with it".
The small waw or yā written after it shows the vowel is lengthened in recitation.

title: Attached pronoun ـهُمْ (them / their)
summary: ـهُمْ (-hum) attached to a word means "them" or "their".
points: قُلُوبِهِمْ = "their hearts".
After an i-sound it is pronounced -him: عَلَيْهِمْ "upon them".
It refers to a group of three or more.

title: Attached pronoun ـكُمْ (you / your, plural)
summary: ـكُمْ (-kum) means "you" or "your" when speaking to a group.
points: رَبَّكُمُ = "your Lord" (addressing many people).
Many verses address humanity or the believers using ـكُمْ.
The singular form is ـكَ (-ka).

title: Attached pronoun ـكَ (you / your, singular)
summary: ـكَ (-ka) means "you" or "your" when addressing one person — often the Prophet ﷺ.
points: رَبِّكَ = "your Lord".
إِلَيْكَ = "to you".
Compare with the plural ـكُمْ.

title: Attached pronoun ـنَا (us / our)
summary: ـنَا (-nā) attached to a noun or preposition means "us" or "our".
points: رَبَّنَا = "our Lord" — it begins many supplications.
عَلَيْنَا = "upon us".
On verbs, -nā can also mean "we did" (covered in a later Juz).

title: Attached pronoun ـهَا (her / it / its)
summary: ـهَا (-hā) refers to something grammatically feminine: "her", "it" or "its".
points: فِيهَا = "in it / therein" — very common when describing Paradise or the earth.
Non-human plurals are often referred to with ـهَا.
So it is not only translated "her".

title: Attached pronoun ـى (me / my)
summary: A final yā (ـى / ـِى) on a noun or verb often means "my" or "me".
points: رَبِّى = "my Lord".
On verbs it appears as ـنِى: "me".
Many supplications of the prophets use this form.

title: بِ — with / in / by
summary: The letter بِ (bi) is a one-letter preposition meaning "with", "in" or "by". It attaches to the next word.
points: بِسْمِ = "in (the) name".
بِٱللَّهِ = "in Allah" (e.g. believing in Allah).
Not every word starting with ب contains this preposition — meaning decides.

title: لِ — for / to
summary: The letter لِ (li) means "for", "to" or "belongs to". It attaches to the next word.
points: لِلَّهِ = "for Allah / belongs to Allah".
With ال the alif drops: لِ + ٱلنَّاسِ → لِلنَّاسِ "for the people".
With pronouns it becomes لَ: لَهُمْ "for them".

title: فَ — so / then
summary: The letter فَ (fa) links a result or sequence: "so", "then", "and so".
points: It attaches to the front of the next word, like وَ.
It often introduces the consequence of what came before.
فَلَا = "so (do) not".

title: Negation with لَا
summary: لَا (lā) means "no" or "not". It can negate a present-tense verb or deny something completely.
points: لَا رَيْبَ = "no doubt".
Before a verb it means "does not": لَا يَعْلَمُونَ "they do not know".
وَلَا = "and not / nor".

title: إِنَّ — indeed
summary: إِنَّ (inna) adds emphasis to a sentence: "indeed" or "truly".
points: It often takes a pronoun: إِنَّهُۥ "indeed, he/it".
The noun after إِنَّ takes the accusative case (-a).
Translators render it as "indeed", "verily" or "surely".

title: Relative pronouns — who / which
summary: ٱلَّذِى (who/which, masculine singular), ٱلَّتِى (feminine) and ٱلَّذِينَ (plural) connect a description to a noun.
points: ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ = "those who believe" — one of the most repeated phrases.
They are always definite and begin with ال.
Notice the doubled lām (لّ).

title: Calling someone: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا
summary: يَا (yā) is used to call or address someone: "O ...". With a definite noun it becomes يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا.
points: يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ = "O mankind".
يَـٰقَوْمِ = "O my people" — frequent in the stories of the prophets.
Look for the long ā written over the yā.

title: Feminine ending ة
summary: Many feminine nouns end in ة (tā marbūṭa), pronounced -ah when pausing.
points: رَحْمَة = "mercy"; جَنَّة = "garden / Paradise".
When joined to the next word it is pronounced -t.
Words like ٱلصَّلَوٰة keep an old spelling with و but are read aṣ-ṣalāh.

title: Sound masculine plural ـُونَ / ـِينَ
summary: Many plurals referring to people end in ـُونَ (-ūna) or ـِينَ (-īna).
points: مُؤْمِن "a believer" → ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ / ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ "the believers".
-ūna is used for the subject; -īna after prepositions or as an object.
The meaning is the same — only the grammatical case changes.

title: The dual — exactly two
summary: Arabic has a special form for exactly two of something, ending in ـَانِ (-āni) or ـَيْنِ (-ayni).
points: جَنَّتَانِ = "two gardens".
English needs the word "two"; Arabic changes the ending instead.
Surah ar-Raḥmān uses many duals.

title: Past tense: they did (ـُوا)
summary: A past-tense verb ending in ـُوا۟ (-ū) means "they did".
points: ءَامَنُوا۟ = "they believed"; كَفَرُوا۟ = "they disbelieved".
The final alif is written but not pronounced.
The same ending appears on commands to a group: قُولُوٓا۟ "say!".

title: Past tense: we did (ـنَا)
summary: On a past-tense verb, ـنَا (-nā) means "we did". Allah often speaks of Himself with the majestic "We".
points: أَنزَلْنَا = "We sent down".
خَلَقْنَا = "We created".
The "royal We" expresses majesty, not number.

title: Past tense: you did (ـتُمْ)
summary: A past-tense verb ending in ـتُمْ (-tum) means "you (all) did".
points: كُنتُمْ = "you were".
Compare with ـتَ (you did, singular).
It often appears in reminders addressed to a community.

title: Present tense with يَـ
summary: Present-tense verbs about "he" or "they" begin with يَـ / يُـ.
points: يَعْلَمُ = "he knows"; يَعْلَمُونَ = "they know".
Adding ـونَ at the end makes it plural.
The present tense also describes habits and the future.

title: كَانَ — was / used to
summary: كَانَ (kāna) means "was". When describing Allah it often expresses a permanent quality: "Allah is ever Forgiving".
points: كَانُوا۟ = "they were / they used to".
Translators often render it "is" for Allah's attributes.
Its predicate takes the accusative case (-an).

title: قَالَ — said / say
summary: قَالَ (qāla) "he said" and the command قُلْ "say!" introduce speech throughout the Quran.
points: قَالُوا۟ = "they said".
قُلْ is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, instructing him what to say.
Many dialogues of the prophets begin with قَالَ.

title: Prepositions with pronouns
summary: Prepositions combine with attached pronouns into one word: عَلَيْهِمْ "upon them", إِلَيْكَ "to you".
points: عَلَىٰ + هُمْ → عَلَيْهِمْ.
مِن + هُ → مِنْهُ "from him / from it".
Spot the preposition at the start and the pronoun at the end.

title: Negation with لَمْ (did not)
summary: لَمْ (lam) + present-tense verb means "did not" — it negates the past.
points: لَمْ يَلِدْ = "He neither begets" (Surah al-Ikhlāṣ).
The verb after لَمْ loses its final vowel (jussive).
أَلَمْ = "did ... not?" — a rhetorical question.

title: Negation with لَن (will never)
summary: لَن (lan) + present-tense verb means "will not / will never" — it negates the future.
points: وَلَن = "and never".
The verb after لَن takes the subjunctive ending (-a).
Compare لَا (does not), لَمْ (did not), لَن (will not).

title: قَدْ — certainly / indeed
summary: قَدْ (qad) before a past-tense verb emphasises that something has truly happened.
points: قَدْ أَفْلَحَ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ = "Certainly will the believers have succeeded".
وَلَقَدْ adds even more emphasis.
Before a present-tense verb it can mean "sometimes" or "surely".
